title: Scaffolding an Existing School Writing Program with Releasing Writers
author: Laura Wood
summary: Laura Wood, a second and third grade teacher, describes adapting a beloved weekly all-school writing tradition using elements of the SRSD approach and Releasing Writers' Self-P(3)OW routine. She explains that the Thursday prompt task is disconnected from content and writing instruction and that some children, including her own son, experience anxiety and overload from generating ideas, spelling, handwriting and illustration at once. With the Head of School's cooperation she obtains the prompt a day early and teaches a Wednesday prewriting lesson covering positive self-talk, pulling apart the prompt, and a T.I.D.E. organizer. She reports that the planning makes Thursday easier for most students and reduces cognitive overload, while noting students still sometimes get stuck and that planning success does not always predict writing success. Because the pieces are posted the same day, she plans to practice editing and revising within content-based writing.
points: A tradition can be kept while its demands are reduced: moving the prompt reveal a day earlier lets teachers front-load planning without changing the event itself.
The prewriting routine has three moves, positive self-talk, pulling apart the prompt, and a T.I.D.E. organizer, each modeled before students write.
Writing ideas down ahead of time lowers cognitive overload for students who struggle with spelling, handwriting or attention, especially when the teacher pre-annotates correct spellings.
Pulling apart the prompt fixed a concrete problem: students no longer returned from the brainstorm unsure what they were supposed to write about.
Results are honest and mixed, since some children still stall in planning or write easily after a weak plan, and full revision cycles must wait for content-based writing.
quotes: Additionally, this Thursday writing task exists on an island, disconnected from both the content students are learning and the writing instruction their grade might otherwise be working through.

I have also seen the toll this writing task takes on some students. My son used to experience intense anxiety that would bring him to tears over the pressure to come up with ideas on the spot. I have seen other students become overwhelmed by the multiple demands of writing: idea generation, handwriting, spelling, punctuation, and illustration—all within a limited amount of time.
I wondered whether I could apply some elements of the SRSD cycle to the existing Thursday writing program to reduce the anxiety and overload some students experience.
Before we started pulling apart the prompt, kids would sometimes return from the all-school prompt reveal and brainstorm session and ask, “What are we writing about again?

Interestingly, sometimes kids struggle to come up with ideas during planning, only to write easily the next day—and vice versa. I have had kids fill out their entire T.I.D.E. organizer, then claim the next day that they don’t know what to write.
I do believe that writing down ideas in a T.I.D.E. organizer helps reduce cognitive overload, especially for students who struggle with spelling, handwriting, and/or attention.

Since the all-school Thursday pieces get illustrated and posted on the same day the kids write them, there is very little time for editing and revision. The editing and revising parts of the POWeR Cycle will therefore need to be practiced when we write about grade-specific content.
